# The Komlos-Sulyok-Szemeredi bound: every finite set of reals has a Sidon subset of size c sqrt n


Call a set of reals a *Sidon set* when all its pairwise sums are distinct: if $a + b = c + d$ with all four in the set, then $\{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$.

The goal is to show that for some absolute constant $c > 0$, every finite set $X$ of positive reals contains a Sidon subset $S$ with $|S| \ge c\sqrt{|X|}$.

This is the lower bound half of [Erdos problem 530](https://www.erdosproblems.com/530), which Riddell posed and which asks for the order of the largest guaranteed Sidon subset. That problem is open: it asks whether the guarantee is asymptotically $N^{1/2}$, and the constant is not known. Komlos, Sulyok, and Szemeredi, *Linear problems in combinatorial number theory*, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 26 (1975) 113-121, settled the order as a case of a general theorem about linear equations. Erdos had previously observed the cube-root lower bound and the matching $(1+o(1))N^{1/2}$ upper bound from $A = \{1, \dots, N\}$. A second and much shorter proof is in Bailleul and Riblet, [arXiv:2605.03181](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03181).

## The exponent is the whole problem

A one-paragraph argument gives $|S| \ge c|X|^{1/3}$: take a Sidon subset $S$ of maximum size, and note that every $x$ outside it satisfies $x = c + d - b$ or $x = (c+d)/2$ for elements of $S$, so $|X| \le 3|S|^3$.

That cube root is not a weak first attempt, it is the ceiling for any argument that only counts. An arithmetic progression of length $n$ has additive energy of order $n^3$, so a probabilistic argument cannot see the difference between it and a generic set. Getting from $1/3$ to $1/2$ requires using the structure of the set, and that is what both published proofs do.

## The idea both proofs share

Compress, then pigeonhole against a known Sidon set.

An arbitrary finite set of reals lacks any arithmetic to work with, so first move it into $\mathbb{Z}$: a finite set spans a finite dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space, and a generic rational functional separates its points while preserving every relation $a + b = c + d$. Then squeeze the resulting integers into an interval of length comparable to their number, keeping a constant fraction of them and keeping the property that a Sidon subset of the image lifts to one of the original. Finally intersect with a translate of the Erdos-Turan Sidon set, which has about $\sqrt{N}$ elements inside $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. A set of size $\Theta(n)$ inside $[1,n]$ meets some translate of a Sidon set of size $\sqrt{n}$ in order $\sqrt{n}$ points, and that intersection is Sidon.

The two proofs differ only in the compression step, and the mission contains both.

## The two routes

The 1975 route compresses in four lemmas driven by a remainder map: choose a modulus $q$ dividing no difference, dilate so that the remainders are small, and observe that a small remainder map preserves $a + b = c + d$. Finding the modulus needs a prime counting bound.

The 2026 route replaces all four with one averaging lemma over a real rotation parameter $\theta$, keeping the elements whose fractional part of $am\theta$ is below $1/2$, where no carry occurs. No prime counting appears anywhere.

## Notes on the formalization

Every item is stated in Mathlib primitives alone, so definition items are unnecessary here. The Sidon condition, the Erdos-Turan construction, and the reduction relation of the 1975 route are all written out at each use.

The published 2026 proof finishes with Singer's 1938 covering of $\mathbb{Z}/(q^2+q+1)\mathbb{Z}$ by $q+1$ Sidon sets. Perfect difference sets are missing from Mathlib, so the mission uses averaging over translates instead. It does the same job at the same order and gives a worse constant, which is fine because the goal asserts only that some $c > 0$ exists.

Two lemmas of the 1975 paper are deliberately absent. A local formalization of Lemma 2 and Lemma 6 turned out to be false as stated, machine-checked in both cases, so neither is offered here as a milestone. Those are errors in that rendering rather than in the paper, and the 2026 route reaches the goal without either. Lemma 1' is absent for the same practical reason: the 2026 route does not need it.

## Bailleul-Riblet Lemma 2.3: compression by a real rotation parameter


For any finite set $A$ of integers and any positive $m$, there is a subset $C$ of $A$ with at least $|A|/2 - |A|^2/(2m)$ elements carrying a map into $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ that is injective on $C$ and preserves $a + b = c + d$.

Put $\varphi_\theta(a) = \lfloor am\theta \rfloor \bmod m$ and keep $B_\theta = \{a \in A : \{am\theta\} < 1/2\}$. On $B_\theta$ two fractional parts sum to less than one, so no carry occurs and $\varphi_\theta$ is additive. Multiplication by a nonzero integer preserves Lebesgue measure mod one, so the average of $|B_\theta|$ over $\theta \in [0,1)$ is at least $|A|/2$, while each colliding pair contributes at most $1/m$. Choose a $\theta$ beating both averages, then delete one element from each colliding pair.

Taking $m$ of order $n$ makes the bound a constant fraction of $n$. The 1975 route reaches the same place through four lemmas and a prime counting bound, and this one statement replaces all of them.

## The Erdos-Turan set has exactly $p$ elements


The set $\{2pk + (k^2 \bmod p) : 0 \le k < p\}$ has exactly $p$ elements.

The defining map is injective on $\{0, \dots, p-1\}$. Since $k^2 \bmod p$ is below $p$, and $p \le 2p$, the value $2pk + (k^2 \bmod p)$ determines $k$ as its quotient by $2p$. Primality is not needed here, only $p > 0$.

## The Erdos-Turan set lives below $2p^2$


Every element of $\{2pk + (k^2 \bmod p) : 0 \le k < p\}$ is less than $2p^2$. The largest is at most $2p(p-1) + (p-1) = 2p^2 - p - 1$.

Bookkeeping, and it is what lets the next statement place the set inside an interval of a prescribed length.

## The Erdos-Turan set is Sidon, for $p$ prime


All pairwise sums of $\{2pk + (k^2 \bmod p) : 0 \le k < p\}$ are distinct when $p$ is prime.

Write the four elements as $2pk_i + r_i$ with $r_i = k_i^2 \bmod p$. Each $r_i$ is below $p$, so $r_1 + r_2 < 2p$ and $r_3 + r_4 < 2p$. Uniqueness of quotient and remainder modulo $2p$ splits the single equation $a_1 + a_2 = a_3 + a_4$ into $k_1 + k_2 = k_3 + k_4$ and $r_1 + r_2 = r_3 + r_4$. The second reads $k_1^2 + k_2^2 \equiv k_3^2 + k_4^2 \pmod p$. So the two pairs have equal sum and equal sum of squares, hence equal sum and equal product, hence they are the roots of the same quadratic over the field $\mathbb{F}_p$.

Primality is exactly what makes $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ a field. The construction genuinely fails at $p = 4, 6, 8, 9, 10$.

## An integer-valued Freiman 2-embedding of a finite set of reals


For every finite set $X$ of reals there is a map $\varphi$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$, injective on $X$, sending every solution of $a + b = c + d$ in $X$ to a solution of the same equation in $\mathbb{Z}$.

From the previous statement by clearing denominators: the functional takes finitely many rational values on $X$, so a single common denominator turns it into an integer-valued map, and scaling a linear map keeps it linear.

## Lemma 3: the second range reduction, down to $n^{3/2}$


There is an absolute $c > 0$ such that any $n$ positive integers bounded by $M$, with $M \le n^3$, reduce to a Sidon-faithful set of at least $cn$ positive integers $b$ with $b^2 \le n^3$, that is $b \le n^{3/2}$.

*Sidon-faithful* is written out: $A$ reduces to $B$ when every Sidon subset of $B$ is matched by a Sidon subset of $A$ at least as large. Note the direction. A reduct is a set that is no easier, so a lower bound proved for $B$ transfers back to $A$.

The bound is squared to stay inside $\mathbb{Z}$ and avoid a real exponent.

## Lemma 4: the third range reduction, down to $n$


There is an absolute $c > 0$ such that any $n$ positive integers bounded by $n^{3/2}$ reduce to a Sidon-faithful set of at least $cn$ positive integers bounded by $n$.

The paper's bound is $3n/\alpha$, which for the Sidon relation is $3n/4$, so $n$ is the weaker requirement and the statement stays true as written.

## Lemma 5: any $n$ positive integers compress into $[1, n]$


There is an absolute $c > 0$ such that any $n$ positive integers reduce to a Sidon-faithful set of at least $cn$ positive integers all at most $n$.

The assembly calls this statement and no other part of the 1975 chain. The paper's constant is $1/(4\alpha^6)$, which is $1/16384$ for the Sidon relation. It is left existential here because that numeral was read off a rough scan, and a statement signed with a constant slightly too strong can never be proved.

## Maximality forces $|X| \le 3|S|^3$


If $S$ is a Sidon subset of $X$ of maximum size, then $|X| \le 3|S|^3$.

Adding any $x$ outside $S$ must break the Sidon property, and since $S$ itself is Sidon the broken relation has to involve $x$. Either $x + b = c + d$ with $b, c, d \in S$, so $x = c + d - b$, at most $|S|^3$ values, or $x + x = c + d$, so $x = (c+d)/2$, at most $|S|^2$ values. With the $|S|$ elements of $S$ that gives $|X| \le |S| + |S|^2 + |S|^3 \le 3|S|^3$, the last step needing $|S| \ge 1$, which holds unless $X$ is empty.

## A Sidon subset of maximum cardinality exists


Every finite set of reals has a Sidon subset no smaller than any other Sidon subset.

There are finitely many subsets, so this is extremality on a finite nonempty family, the empty set being always available. Short, and it is what makes "take a maximal Sidon subset" a legal move in the next statement.

## A $\mathbb{Q}$-linear functional injective on a finite set of reals


For every finite set $X$ of reals there is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ that is injective on $X$.

$X$ is finite, so its $\mathbb{Q}$-span is finite dimensional. Pick a basis, and take the functional whose value is the coordinate vector read as an integer in base $M$, for $M$ past every coordinate difference. Extend to all of $\mathbb{R}$ by a Hamel basis, which is where the axiom of choice enters.

## Remark 3: a small remainder map preserves $a+b=c+d$


If every $a$ in $A$ is written $a = k(a)q + r(a)$ with the remainder small, $4|r(a)| < q$, then $a \mapsto r(a)$ preserves the relation $a + b = c + d$.

The two remainder sums each have absolute value below $q/2$, so their difference has absolute value below $q$; it is also a multiple of $q$, so it is zero.

The constant 4 is the paper's $\alpha$ for the Sidon relation, whose coefficient vector is $(1, 1, -1, -1)$, and every later step of the 1975 route reduces to an application of this remark at some modulus.

## The cube-root bound: a Sidon subset of size $c|X|^{1/3}$


There is an absolute $c > 0$ such that every finite set of reals has a Sidon subset of size at least $c|X|^{1/3}$. Immediate from the previous two with $c = 3^{-1/3}$.

This is the ceiling for any purely probabilistic argument, because an arithmetic progression of length $n$ really does have additive energy of order $n^3$. Getting from $1/3$ to $1/2$ is the whole problem.

## A Sidon subset of $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ of size at least $\sqrt{N}/4$


For every $N$ there is a Sidon set inside $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ with at least $\sqrt{N}/4$ elements.

Two regimes. For $N \le 144$ the fixed set $\{0, 1, 3\}$ already has three elements and $\sqrt{144}/4 = 3$, and for $N < 4$ the singleton $\{0\}$ does. For $N > 144$ take $m = \lfloor\sqrt{N/2}\rfloor/2$ and apply Bertrand's postulate to get a prime $p$ with $m < p \le 2m$. Then $2p^2 \le N$, so the previous statement puts the Erdos-Turan set inside the interval, and $p > m$ beats $\sqrt{N}/4$.

Every later milestone pigeonholes a set against this one. It is also the one place in the development where a Sidon set is constructed; everywhere else a Sidon set is found inside something given.

## The Komlos-Sulyok-Szemeredi bound: a Sidon subset of size $c\sqrt{|X|}$


There is an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that every finite set $X$ of positive reals contains a subset $S$ all of whose pairwise sums are distinct, with $|S| \ge c\sqrt{|X|}$.

A set with all pairwise sums distinct is a *Sidon set*. The condition is written out at each use: for $a, b, c, d \in S$ with $a + b = c + d$, either $a = c$ and $b = d$, or $a = d$ and $b = c$. Repeats are allowed on both sides, so $a = b$ is not excluded; what is excluded is two genuinely different unordered pairs sharing a sum.

The constant is quantified outside the $\forall X$, so it is absolute and there is no "for $|X|$ large enough" escape hatch. Small $X$ is covered by taking $c$ small, since a one-element set is Sidon. Positivity of the elements is never used, because the Sidon condition is translation invariant; it stays because the problem states it.

## Pull a Sidon set back from the integer image


Given $\varphi$ injective on $X$ and preserving $a + b = c + d$, any Sidon subset $T$ of the image $\varphi(X)$ comes from a Sidon subset of $X$ of at least the same size, namely its preimage in $X$.

Only the forward direction of the transfer is ever needed. That is why the embedding is asked to preserve the relation rather than to reflect it.

## Some translate of $B$ meets $A$ in $|A||B|/m$ points


For $A$ and $B$ inside $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$, some translate $B + i$ meets $A$ in at least $|A||B|/m$ points. Double counting over all $m$ translates.

This stands in for Singer's 1938 covering of $\mathbb{Z}/(q^2+q+1)\mathbb{Z}$ by $q+1$ Sidon sets, which the published proof uses and which is not available here. It does the same job at the same order, since a Sidon set of size about $\sqrt{m}$ averaged over $m$ translates meets a set of size $s$ in about $s/\sqrt{m}$ points. The constant comes out worse than Singer's $1/(3\sqrt{3})$, and the goal only claims that some $c > 0$ exists.

## Milestone A1: a maximum Sidon subset exists


Every finite set of reals has a Sidon subset no smaller than any other. Finitely many subsets, so this is extremality on a finite nonempty family, the empty set being always available. It is what makes "take a maximal Sidon subset" a legal move.

## Milestone A2: maximality forces $|X| \le 3|S|^3$


Adding any element outside a maximum Sidon subset $S$ must break the Sidon property, and the broken relation has to involve the new element. That gives $x = c + d - b$ or $x = (c+d)/2$ for elements of $S$, so at most $|S|^3 + |S|^2$ outsiders. Formalize the counting as an injection into $S^3 \sqcup S^2$.

## Milestone A3: the cube-root bound


An absolute $c > 0$ with a Sidon subset of size $c|X|^{1/3}$ in every finite set of reals, immediate from A1 and A2. Worth stating on its own because it is the ceiling for any purely counting argument: an arithmetic progression of length $n$ has additive energy of order $n^3$.

The map $k \mapsto 2pk + (k^2 \bmod p)$ is injective on $\{0, \dots, p-1\}$, because the remainder is below $p \le 2p$ so the quotient by $2p$ recovers $k$. Primality is not needed, only $p > 0$.

## Milestone B2: the Erdos-Turan set is Sidon


The hardest leaf of the construction. Uniqueness of quotient and remainder mod $2p$ splits one equation into $k_1 + k_2 = k_3 + k_4$ and $k_1^2 + k_2^2 \equiv k_3^2 + k_4^2 \pmod p$, so the two pairs have equal sum and equal product and are the roots of the same quadratic over $\mathbb{F}_p$. Primality is exactly what makes that a field. At $p = 4, 6, 8, 9, 10$ the construction genuinely fails.

## Milestone B3: the Erdos-Turan set lives below $2p^2$


The largest element is at most $2p(p-1) + (p-1)$. Bookkeeping, and it is what lets B4 place the set inside an interval of prescribed length.

## Milestone B4: a Sidon subset of $[0, N)$ of size $\sqrt{N}/4$


Assemble B1 to B3 with Bertrand's postulate: for $N > 144$ pick a prime $p$ between $m$ and $2m$ for $m = \lfloor\sqrt{N/2}\rfloor/2$, so that $2p^2 \le N$. A finite set of reals spans a finite dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space, so a functional reading the coordinate vector in a large enough base separates its points. Extending to all of $\mathbb{R}$ needs a Hamel basis, which is where choice enters.

Clear denominators in C1. The functional takes finitely many rational values on the set, so one common denominator makes it integer-valued, and scaling a linear map keeps it linear. This is the step that turns a problem about arbitrary reals into a problem about integers.

## Milestone C3: pull a Sidon set back to the reals


A Sidon subset of the integer image lifts to a Sidon subset of the original set of at least the same size. Only the forward direction of the embedding is ever needed. That is why C2 asks the map to preserve $a + b = c + d$ rather than to reflect it.

The workhorse of the 1975 route. If the remainders satisfy $4|r(a)| < q$ then the two remainder sums differ by less than $q$ and by a multiple of $q$, so by nothing. The constant 4 is the paper's $\alpha$ for the Sidon relation, whose coefficient vector is $(1,1,-1,-1)$.
